summary: Proposes a structured format for sending documents that mix several kinds of content, such as text and other media, between computer mail systems. It lays out how a document and its parts are described so different systems can exchange them.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines a way to organize a message's fields and body. The body can contain text, graphics, fax, or voice, with rules for how its parts relate in time.

questions: how to send multimedia documents by email in 1980
subtitle: A structured format for messages that combine text, graphics, facsimile, and voice.

tldr.problem: The Internet Message Protocol needed a document format that could represent both ordinary message fields and bodies containing more than one kind of media.
tldr.mechanism: A document is a list of named fields, and its body can hold media structures arranged sequentially, simultaneously, or independently.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines a flexible document representation and examples, while noting that each medium still needs its own data format.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 767's status as Unknown and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC describes its first edition as a request for comments and suggestions.

sections.title: Documents and Message Fields
sections.content:
RFC 767 defines a format for structured multimedia documents carried with the Internet Message Protocol. That protocol's message has an identification, a command, and a document; this RFC specifies the document.

A document is a property list of named fields such as DATE, SENDER, SUBJECT, and BODY. The body may be a simple text element or a structured collection of media. The format allows new fields, though a receiver may not understand every added field.
sections.plainLanguage: A message document is a set of labeled pieces, such as sender, subject, and body. The body may contain plain text or a structured mix of media.

sections.title: Mailboxes and Document Objects
sections.content:
The RFC defines objects used in fields, including dates, addresses, mailboxes, message identifiers, and pointers. A mailbox is a property list that can identify a recipient through network, host, user, and other details. It may also represent a distribution group. The minimum document includes DATE, SENDER, SUBJECT, and BODY.

Dates follow a specified numeric representation with a time-zone offset. The document can also include FROM, TO, CC, BCC, REPLY-TO, COMMENTS, MESSAGE-ID, REFERENCES, and KEYWORDS. A pointer describes how to locate and access information stored outside the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Each field has a defined kind of value. A recipient can be named with account details or a group name, and a pointer can describe outside data.

sections.title: Multimedia Bodies and Presentation Order
sections.content:
Small presentation elements combine media structures, and presentation descriptors specify their time relationship. SEQUENTIAL means items appear one at a time in order. SIMULTANEOUS means parallel presentation. INDEPENDENT means the items have no required order.

The listed media are TEXT, VOICE, FACSIMILE, and GRAPHICS. The RFC gives structures for each: for example, voice data identifies its vocoder and protocol, while facsimile identifies a device and protocol. It says standard data formats must be defined for the media. Its examples show simple text and a body combining text with voice and graphics.
sections.plainLanguage: A body can tell a receiver to show items in order, at the same time, or without a fixed order. Each media item also identifies how its data is represented.
